rationale: The book strongly establishes that righteousness can denote right conduct and that Revelation 19’s linen consists of righteous acts. It does not establish that performed right-living is the uniform substance of righteousness across the supplied texts. The strongest contextual reading better distinguishes God’s own rectitude, human obedient conduct, righteous acts, and the righteousness reckoned to the ungodly apart from works. Romans 4 in particular describes a forensic or relational credit accompanying forgiveness, not performed obedience merely received from a different source. The book preserves its uniform definition only by recasting faith as the righteous act being counted, despite Paul’s explicit contrast with working, and by treating distinct terms and contexts as one invariant referent.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is substantively right-living: for humans under God, it is obedience to his commandments or righteous conduct, even when it is given or reckoned by grace rather than earned.
book_secondary_elaborations: God is right-living by definition because his ways establish the measure of right.
Righteousness is the garment woven from righteous acts, especially the law kept and visibly worn.
The wedding garment in Matthew 22 is identified with the bride’s fine linen of righteous acts in Revelation 19:8.
Grace changes the source and mode of receiving righteousness but not its behavioral substance.
Garments signify the covenant lived out; nakedness signifies exposed covenant breach.
Righteous garments may be stained by sin and must be washed and kept clean.
The armor of God is God’s own symbolic clothing, ultimately understood as putting on Christ.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Righteousness has related but contextually distinct senses: God’s rectitude and saving justice, human conformity to his commands, and—especially in Romans 4 and Philippians 3—a favorable standing reckoned by God through faith rather than a body of performed right-living. Revelation 19:8 explicitly identifies the linen with righteous acts, but that plural term and symbolic setting do not redefine every occurrence of righteousness as conduct.
counter_core_identification: In the Pauline reckoning texts, righteousness is principally a God-granted forensic or relational status, while obedient conduct is a distinct ethical sense found in texts such as Deuteronomy 6:25 and 1 John 3:7.
material_core_denial: Righteousness is not uniformly performed right-living in substance; in Romans 4 it is reckoned to an ungodly person without works as part of forgiveness and non-imputation of sin.
counter_case: Deuteronomy 6:25, Psalm 119:172, and 1 John 3:7 plainly support an ethical use: observing commandments and doing righteousness constitute righteous conduct.

Romans 4:4-8 deliberately contrasts working for a debt with righteousness being credited to one who does not work and whom God identifies as ungodly. David’s explanation is forgiveness and non-imputation of sin, naturally indicating changed standing rather than already-performed right-living.

The book’s claim that faith is counted as the right response does not make the credited righteousness identical to a life of righteous acts. The accepted prior finding that living faith is enacted through obedience concerns the character of faith, not the lexical identity of righteousness in every context.

Philippians 3:9 contrasts two kinds or grounds of righteousness—one’s own from law and that from God through faith. A God-given standing or relationship explains this contrast directly, whereas calling both the same behavioral substance but with different sources is possible yet not textually required.

Revelation 19:8 uses the plural dikaiomata and explicitly glosses the linen as the saints’ righteous acts. That securely interprets this garment, but also supports contextual differentiation between righteous deeds and the singular righteousness reckoned in Romans 4.

God’s righteousness in Deuteronomy 32:4 and Psalm 145:17 is his justice, rectitude, and faultless action. Calling this ‘Right-Living’ is a serviceable paraphrase, but it does not prove a uniform behavioral definition for forensic uses involving sinners.
book_explanatory_advantages: It gives a direct and compelling account of Deuteronomy 6:25, Psalm 119:172, and 1 John 3:7.
It takes Revelation 19:8’s explicit identification of fine linen with righteous acts seriously.
It prevents grace from being construed as moral indifference or as God declaring persistent evil to be good.
It coheres with the accepted findings that saving belief and living faith involve obedient submission rather than bare assent.
It integrates garment, defilement, washing, nakedness, covenant, and conduct into a substantial biblical motif.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It preserves the explicit ‘without works’ and ‘justifieth the ungodly’ language of Romans 4 without redefining credited righteousness as performed right-living.
It accounts for David’s explanation of imputation in terms of forgiveness, covered sins, and non-imputation of sin.
It distinguishes dikaiosyne, dikaiomata, divine righteousness, ethical righteousness, and forensic reckoning according to their immediate contexts.
It can affirm every ethical text cited by the book without extending that sense into contexts that expressly contrast reckoning with works.
It requires fewer unsupported links, particularly between Matthew 22’s unidentified wedding garment and Revelation 19’s collective bridal linen.
It explains why Christian interpretations commonly retain both right standing and right conduct rather than reducing either category to the other.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Romans 4:5-6 describes God as justifying the ungodly and imputing righteousness ‘without works.’ If righteousness is identified substantively with performed right-living, the passage credits the substance of performed conduct precisely where such works are excluded.

Romans 4:7-8 explains the blessed reckoning through forgiven iniquities, covered sins, and sin not being imputed. Those are changes in liability and standing; they are not descriptions of commandments performed.

Revelation 19:8 explicitly says dikaiomata, righteous acts, whereas Romans 4 speaks of righteousness being imputed. Treating the two expressions as one invariant behavioral substance obscures rather than explains this grammatical and contextual distinction.
unresolved_objections: The forensic counter must not sever justified status from the obedient life intrinsic to living faith; the accepted prior findings rule out bare assent as saving faith.
Revelation 19:8 and 1 John 3:7 give conduct a more central role in final judgment and discipleship than some purely imputed-righteousness formulations acknowledge.
The precise relationship between God’s reckoning, union with Christ, subsequent transformation, and final righteous deeds is not fully settled by the supplied excerpts.
The book’s broader garment theology may remain valuable even though it does not establish a uniform lexical definition of righteousness.
